There are numerous types of French spoken around the world, broadly classified by geography and linguistic features [d5]. The most widely recognized standard is Parisian French, also called Metropolitan or International French, which is considered the prestige form and is most commonly taught in schools [d1][d6][d8][d9]. Outside of France, major varieties include Quebec French (Québécois) in Canada — which features distinct pronunciation (e.g., "t" and "d" shifting to "ts" and "dz") and English-influenced vocabulary — as well as Belgian French, Swiss French, and Algerian French [d3][d5][d6][d9]. In the Caribbean and Americas, Haitian Creole and Louisiana Creole are French-based creole languages, while Ivoirian French serves as an official language in Ivory Coast [d2][d3][d9]. Within France itself, regional varieties include Marseillais French in the south, and broader dialect groups such as the northern Langues d'oïl and the southern Occitan dialects, alongside other regional minority languages of Romance and non-Romance origin [d4][d7][d8].
